This theory, created and developed mostly by {{ill|Tendai|az|Tenday|bg|Тендай|cs|Tendai|da|Tendai Skolen|de|Tendai-shū|es|Tendai|fa|تندای|fi|Tendai|fr|Tendai|hu|Tendai|id|Tendai|it|Buddismo Tendai|ko|천태종 (일본)|ml|തെൻദായ്|nl|Tendai|no|Tendai-shū|pl|Tendai|pt|Tendai|ro|Tendai|ru|Тэндай|sh|Tendai|sr|Tendaj|sv|Tendai|ta|டெண்டாய்|tr|Tendai|uk|Секта Тендай|zu|Tendai|qid=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} monks, was never systematized but was nonetheless very pervasive and influential.<ref>* {{cite web   |url=http://www.univie.ac.at/rel_jap/gesch/honjisuijaku.htm   |title=Honji suijaku: Die Angleichung von Buddhas und Kami   |last=Scheid, Bernhard   |author-link=Bernhard Scheid   |language=de   |access-date=June 13, 2011}}</ref> The book had thereafter great influence over literature and the arts.<ref name="kojien"/>

==History==
The book is believed to have been written during the late Nanboku-chō period, either during the {{ill|Bunna|de|Bunna|fa|بوننا|fr|Ère Bunna|ja|文和|ko|분나|ru|Бунна|simple|Bunna|sr|Буна (ера)|sv|Bunna|tr|Bunna|zh|文和|qid=Q1146252|lt=Bunna}} or the {{ill|Enbun|de|Enbun|fa|انبون (دوره)|fr|Ère Enbun|ja|延文|ko|엔분|ru|Эмбун|simple|Enbun|sr|Енбун|sv|Enbun|tr|Enbun|zh|延文|qid=Q1145071|lt=Enbun}} era.<ref name=yahoo>{{cite web|last=Murakami|first=Manabu|title=Shintōshū|url=http://100.yahoo.co.jp/detail/%E7%A5%9E%E9%81%93%E9%9B%86/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121209055811/http://100.yahoo.co.jp/detail/%E7%A5%9E%E9%81%93%E9%9B%86/|url-status=dead|archive-date=9 December 2012|work=Shogakukan Encyclopedia|publisher=Yahoo Japan|access-date=15 June 2011|language=ja}}</ref> It carries the note {{nihongo|Agui-saku|安居院作|extra=made by Agui}} but who exactly wrote it is unclear. Búddà|za|Fozgyau|zea|Boeddhisme|zgh|ⵜⴰⴱⵓⴷⵉⵜ|zh|佛教|zh_classical|佛教|zh_min_nan|Hu̍t-kàu|zh_yue|佛教|zu|UbuBudha|qid=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}. This theory was never systematized but became nonetheless the most important tool through which foreign Buddhism was reconciled with local ''kami'' beliefs. The book illustrates it through tales dedicated to various shrines and to the Buddhist gods which are the true nature of the ''kami'' they enshrine.<ref name="yahoo"/> It deals mostly with shrines located west of [[Tonegawa, Kōzuke|Tonegawa]] in [[:en:Kōzuke province|Kōzuke province]] (like Akagi Daimyōjin, Ikaho Daimyōjin and Komochiyama Daimyōjin), the [[Kumano shrine|Kumano Sanzan]] and other [[:en:Kantō|Kantō]] shrines, explaining the reason for their ''kami's''  rebirths, and telling tales about their previous lives.<ref name="yahoo"/>

The common point of the tales is that before being reborn as a tutelary ''kami'' of an area, a person must first be born and suffer there as a human being. The suffering is mostly caused by relationships with relatives, especially wives or husbands.<ref name="yahoo"/>

The book had a great impact on the literature and arts of the following centuries.
